title: Protecting the fluoride reservoir
html:
‘Spit, don’t rinse’ is familiar oral health advice, but understanding the fluoride reservoir can help dental professionals give patients more precise, evidence-based guidance.

For years, ‘spit, don’t rinse’ has been one of the simplest oral health messages to communicate to patients. Yet those four words can leave an important question unanswered: rinse with what?

Current Delivering Better Oral Health (2025) guidance provides a more precise message. Adults should brush at least twice daily with toothpaste containing 1,350-1,500 ppm fluoride and spit after brushing rather than rinsing with water, to avoid diluting the fluoride concentration.

Why fluoride retention matters

During brushing with fluoride toothpaste, fluoride accumulates in ‘reservoirs’ within the mouth, from which it can subsequently be released over time, helping to maintain fluoride availability after the toothbrush has been put away (Sköld et al, 2012).

Rinsing with water immediately afterwards can interfere with this process. Research cited by Sköld and colleagues (2012) found that greater volumes of water used after brushing were associated with lower fluoride retention in the oral cavity.

This supports the familiar recommendation to spit out excess toothpaste rather than washing the remaining fluoride away. However, the evidence also highlights an important distinction between rinsing with water and rinsing with a fluoride-containing mouthwash.

Adding to the reservoir

In a randomised, investigator-blind crossover study, 30 participants brushed with 1,450 ppm fluoride toothpaste before either rinsing with a 225 ppm fluoride mouthwash, rinsing with a 500 ppm fluoride mouthwash or not rinsing at all (Sköld et al, 2012).

Both fluoride mouthwashes significantly increased salivary fluoride retention over the following 60 minutes compared with not rinsing. Mean area-under-the-curve values were 380 for the 225 ppm fluoride mouthwash and 626 for the 500 ppm mouthwash, compared with 237 when participants did not rinse. All pairwise differences were statistically significant (p<0.01) (Sköld et al, 2012).

The study therefore demonstrates that, at the concentrations studied, using a fluoride mouthwash immediately after brushing significantly increased salivary fluoride retention compared with not rinsing.

Making every recommendation count

Current UK guidance recognises a role for daily fluoride mouthrinse for those at increased caries risk (Delivering Better Oral Health, 2025), while evidence also supports the adjunctive use of mouthrinse to help manage plaque accumulation (Chapple et al, 2015).

Published evidence adds important nuance to our understanding of what happens when a fluoride mouthwash is used immediately after brushing.

Sköld et al (2012) demonstrated that rinsing with a fluoride mouthwash containing 225 ppm or 500 ppm fluoride significantly increased salivary fluoride retention compared with simply spitting out the toothpaste and not rinsing.

This distinction matters.

For dental professionals, this provides an opportunity to give patients more informed advice about their oral hygiene routines and the role that an evidence-based fluoride mouthwash may play according to individual need.

References

  • Chapple ILC, Van der Weijden F, Doerfer C, et al (2015)Primary prevention of periodontitis: managing gingivitis. Journal of Clinical Periodontology; 42(S16): S71–S76.
  • Delivering Better Oral Health: an evidence-based toolkit for prevention. Chapter 2: Summary guidance tables for dental teams. Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, Department of Health and Social Care, NHS England: 2025.
  • Sköld UM, Birkhed D, Ellwood R (2012) Effect of post-brushing mouthwash solutions on salivary fluoride retention – study 1. Journal of Clinical Dentistry; 23(3): 97–100.
